newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope defends Catholicism's influence in Poland.
newsitem.headline: Pope defends Catholicism's influence in Poland.

text.p: Pope John Paul told his countrymen on Friday that, despite recent social changes in Poland, Catholicism was embedded in its national identity and must remain the force guiding the country's future.

After a day of rest, the 77-year-old Pope resumed public appearances with a big open-air mass in the southern mountain resort of Zakopane, where he put two 19th and 20th century nuns on the road to sainthood in the Roman Catholic Church.

There, in the idyllic area were he used to relax and meditate as a young man, bishop and cardinal, he touched on one of the issues dividing Poles as they prepare for parliamentary elections due in September -- the influence of the Church.

In his sermon before some 200,000 people gathered around a hill used as a ski jump, the Pope referred to a controversy that erupted in Poland after the 1989 fall of communism over the display of crucifixes in schools and public offices.

The first non-communist governments allowed a return of crucifixes in public buildings as a symbol of Poland's predominantly Catholic heritage and as a tribute to the role the Church had played in Marxism's downfall.
This decision was contested by the leftist opposition and some intellectuals who wanted a clearer separation of Church and state. But the crucifixes have remained on the walls.

"We thank divine providence that the crucifix has returned to schools, public offices and hospitals," the Pope told the crowd from a wooden altar platform shaped like a chalet typical of the area of sweeping vistas and majestic peaks.
"May it ever remain there. May it remind us of our Christian dignity and national identity, what we are and where we are going and what our roots are," he said.
The Church enjoyed great prestige before 1989 among Poles, 90 percent of whom are at least nominally Catholic, because of its defence of human rights during communist rule.

But when pro-Catholic parties won power in democratic Poland, their moves to restore property and grant privileges to the Church aroused resentment, which was skilfully used by the ex-communists to help their election victory in 1993.

Now the pro-Catholic Solidarity Election Action (AWS) -- an alliance of more than 30 small right-wing and centrist parties clustered around the Solidarity trade union -- has been looking for a Papal message that can translate to votes at the ballot box.

The AWS demands that parliament ratify a treaty with the Vatican, known as the concordat, which was signed by a former government to regulate the Church's status in Poland, but which has since been delayed by leftists in parliament.

The two nuns who were beatified by the Pope at the Zakopane mass were Maria Karlowska, who set up a home in the 19th century to help prostitutes, the poor and the disinherited, and Maria Jablonska, who founded an order of nuns to help the poor before she died in 1940.
The Pope, who seems to been invigorated by the scent and feel of his homeland since his arrival on Saturday, was not scheduled for any further public engagements on Friday.

Aides said he would most likely meet old friends in the church-owned chalet where Vatican and Polish security are jealously guarding his privacy, or be taken to an isolated mountain area for outdoor rest and prayer.
The Pope, an avid hiker and skiier before he broke his leg in 1994, was taken by helicopter for a airborne tour over favourite mountain walks and a river where he used to canoe.
He returns to Rome on Tuesday at the end of the 11-day trip,
